findings.title: Credential key stored as the full safeParse result, not the parsed data
findings.body: The new helper `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the `safeParse` envelope (`{ success, data }`). The Google Calendar service assigns that envelope directly to `key` and persists it: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema); await prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key } });`. After the next refresh, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will be parsing an object of shape `{ success: true, data: { access_token, refresh_token, ... } }`, which fails every required field check, so the credential becomes permanently invalid. Other call sites (office365calendar, salesforce, zoom) correctly read `.data`; this is the lone regression. The function should return just the data, or the call site should be `data: { key: key.data }`.

findings.title: Missing refresh token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the parsed token response does not contain a `refresh_token`, the helper assigns `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` and stores the credential. The literal string "refresh_token" is not a valid OAuth refresh token, so on the very next refresh the provider will respond with `invalid_grant`, the credential will be invalidated, and (because it is now in the local DB) the user is stuck with a non-recoverable integration. The comment indicates the self-hoster's endpoint may return only `access_token` and `expiry_date`, in which case this branch is hit on every refresh. The function should refuse to mint a credential without a real refresh token, or fall back to the previously stored one.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema computed keys both evaluate to the same literal string
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()` use a Zod instance's default `Object.prototype.toString`, which returns the string `"[object Object]"` (zod does not override `toString` on ZodString / ZodOptional). Both expressions therefore evaluate to the same string. In an object literal the second property overwrites the first, so the schema collapses to `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), "[object Object]": z.unknown().optional() })`. The schema does not match the obvious intent ("any string key with a number value, plus any other properties"); it accepts any object that happens to have an `access_token` string and no other validation of the rest of the OAuth response. With this minimum schema in effect, callers will silently accept malformed token responses from the self-hoster's endpoint and store them, which then fails on subsequent use.

findings.title: Time-of-check/time-of-use race in credential upsert
findings.body: The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst` and then either `update` or `create` based on the result. There is no unique constraint on `(userId, appId)` in the credential model (the comment at line 61 even acknowledges this), and nothing atomic here. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both see no existing credential and both attempt `create`, so one will fail with a unique-constraint / duplicate-key error (or succeed in creating a second row). The function does not wrap this in a transaction, does not use `upsert`, and does not catch the duplicate error and retry as an update. Result is a 500 for one of the two callers and/or duplicate credentials in the DB.

findings.title: No HTTP method check; webhook accepts GET, HEAD, etc.
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method`. Anything other than POST will reach the body validation step, where `req.body` is typically undefined for GET, and `z.object({...}).parse(undefined)` will throw a ZodError, producing a 500 (and possibly leaking the expected schema in the response). The endpoint is a state-mutating webhook; it should explicitly `if (req.method !== 'POST') return res.status(405).json({ message: 'Method not allowed' })`.

findings.title: symmetricDecrypt / JSON.parse failures are unhandled
findings.body: The block `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""))` can throw in several ways: empty encryption key (falls back to `""`), wrong key, ciphertext tampered or not actually encrypted with this key, or successfully decrypted bytes that are not valid JSON. None of these are caught. A misconfigured self-hoster or any malformed payload will produce an unhandled 500, and the original ZodError from line 31 is similarly uncaught (would also 500 with the schema details). Both should be caught and returned as 4xx with a generic message, and the decryption/key-mismatch path should be logged.

findings.title: Decrypted payload is stored as the credential key with no shape validation
findings.body: After decrypting, the handler assigns `key: keys` to the credential, where `keys` is the result of `JSON.parse` (typed as `any`). There is no schema check that the decrypted value has the shape the downstream app expects (e.g. `{ access_token, refresh_token, expiry_date, ... }` for Google). Anyone holding the webhook secret and the encryption key can therefore overwrite an end-user's credential with arbitrary JSON. A compromised or buggy parent application could silently break a user's integration, and the next refresh would feed this malformed object into the per-app schemas (each of which has its own idea of the shape). Validate the parsed object against the target app's credential schema before persisting.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string equality
findings.body: The secret check is `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. For a shared webhook secret the practical risk is low, but a remote attacker who can repeatedly send crafted requests and measure response times can in principle narrow down the secret byte-by-byte. Compare with a constant-time function such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

findings.title: Redundant prisma.app lookup; appStoreMetadata is the source of truth
findings.body: The PR description states the parent's app store is the source of truth for apps, but this handler queries `prisma.app.findUnique({ where: { slug: reqBody.appSlug } })` and 404s if the local `app` row is missing. The `app` table is only populated by the app metadata sync (`CRON_ENABLE_APP_SYNC`, etc.), so a self-hoster whose env is fine but whose app sync has not run yet will see 404 for every valid slug. The very next line uses `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]`, which is the in-memory registry that the database is synced from, so the DB hit is unnecessary. Replace with `appStoreMetadata[reqBody.appSlug as keyof typeof appStoreMetadata]` and a single 404 if undefined.

findings.title: APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is a string, not a boolean
findings.body: `export const APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED = process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY;` uses `&&` rather than `!!(...)`. The value is therefore the encryption-key string (a non-empty string is truthy, so the constant is the second operand's value), or `undefined` when either is missing. Every use site does a truthy check, so behaviour accidentally works today, but the type is wrong, the name is misleading, and a stricter consumer that does `=== true` or `Boolean(APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED)` would break. Should be `!!(process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY)`.

findings.title: Outbound refresh request to self-hoster endpoint is unauthenticated
findings.body: When credential sharing is enabled, the Cal.com server POSTs to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the form body. There is no shared-secret header, no mTLS, no signature, and no per-user token; the only way the self-hoster can know the request is legitimate is by IP allowlist. The self-hoster's endpoint must return a valid access token to that Cal.com, so anyone able to reach the URL can mint tokens for arbitrary (calcomUserId, appSlug) pairs that the parent will then trust. Add an HMAC over the body using a shared secret (the same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` already configured would be the natural fit), or otherwise authenticate the caller.

findings.title: Outbound refresh fetch has no timeout and no error handling
findings.body: The `fetch` to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no `AbortController` / timeout, no try/catch, and no response-status check. If the self-hoster's endpoint is slow, the entire Cal.com request handler that triggered the refresh hangs (booking flow, calendar lookup, etc.); if it returns 5xx or fails DNS, the unhandled rejection bubbles up. Wrap in a timeout (e.g. 5–10s) and treat any non-2xx or network error as a refresh failure (which should invalidate the credential, the way direct-OAuth refreshes already do).

findings.title: statusText-based HTTP check instead of response.ok
findings.body: Salesforce's refresh path checks `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError(...)`. `response.statusText` is an arbitrary reason phrase that the server may or may not send and that `fetch` does not always populate; the canonical way is `if (!response.ok)`. As written, a 4xx/5xx whose `statusText` happens to be `"OK"` (some proxies / Salesforce errors do this) would be treated as success and the response body parsed as a token, with `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then `reject`ing; in the opposite direction, a perfectly valid 200 with statusText `""` (HTTP/2, some servers) would always be rejected. Use `response.ok` and read the body for the real error.

findings.title: Salesforce access token is refreshed on every API call
findings.body: `getClient` is called from the constructor, before any expiry check, and unconditionally POSTs to the Salesforce token endpoint. There is no `isExpired` / `isTokenValid` short-circuit like the other integrations (Google, HubSpot, Lark, O365, Zoho) use. Every single Salesforce interaction (contact search, create event, update event, delete event) now incurs a synchronous network round trip to Salesforce, plus a credential-row write. Add the usual expiry check on `credentialKey.expires_in`/`expiry_date` and only call the refresh path when actually needed.

findings.title: Helper returns the safeParse envelope, callers silently mis-use it
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full `{ success, data }` object from `safeParse`, then performs a mutation (`refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = ...`) on the parsed result. Two of the four call sites correctly take `.data`, but the Google Calendar call site does not and the inconsistency already produced a high-severity regression there. The contract should be "return the data (after validation)", and the function should not be the place where the literal `refresh_token` is fabricated. Either return `data` directly or rename and document that callers must read `.data`.

findings.title: Header name is documented as lowercase but the code does not normalize
findings.body: The .env.example comment says "This is the header name that will be used to verify the webhook secret. Should be in lowercase." The handler reads `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]`. In Next.js / Node, incoming HTTP header names are lower-cased, but the configured `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` is used as-is to index into `req.headers`. If a self-hoster sets it to anything but lower-case, the lookup silently fails and the request is rejected as 403 with no actionable message. Either enforce/document lowercase validation at startup, or normalize the configured name with `.toLowerCase()` before use.

findings.title: New webhook endpoint and OAuth helpers have no tests
findings.body: The PR description explicitly says "I haven't added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works". The two new endpoints (`/api/webhook/app-credential`), the two new helpers (`parseRefreshTokenResponse`, `refreshOAuthTokens`), and the new `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` constant together introduce a security-sensitive credential-syncing path. At a minimum: (1) webhook secret check accepts correct header and rejects wrong/absent; (2) Zod schema rejects malformed bodies and gives a 400; (3) symmetricDecrypt with wrong key is caught and is a 4xx, not a 500; (4) race against a concurrent identical webhook does not 500 (or returns idempotently); (5) `parseRefreshTokenResponse` does not silently fabricate a refresh_token; (6) `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` is a boolean, not a string. None of these are covered.
